ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics: Data collection of the ALLS was approved by the ethics committee of the five partner universities and at the national levels in Kenya and Namibia.
Participants were recruited with the help of local research assistants who reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools.
After providing informed consent, participants completed surveys on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants' devices, or on paper.
Assessment waves (henceforward called W1 to W9) took place every 6 months, when participants were re-contacted by text, email, or in person via the local research assistants.
At W1, participants were on average 18.30 years old (SD = 0.72).
Participants were approximately equally distributed across the three countries (Kenya: 34%, Namibia: 33%, South Africa: 33%), 56% of the sample were female, and 67% had high school level education.
These samples sizes of the event groups refer to "robust event occurrences", meaning that participants had to report a respective life change at two consecutive assessments.

table.text: When preregistering the study (i.e., before determining our final sample size), we conducted approximative power analyses based on paired t-tests using the R package pwr (Champely, 2006). These power analyses indicated sufficient power (1 -β = 0.80, α = .01) to identify very small event-related changes (d = 0.10) for events with a sample size of n = 1,172, small event-related changes (d = 0.20) for events with a sample size of n = 296, medium eventrelated changes (d = 0.41) for events with n = 73, and strong event-related changes (d = 0.63) for events with n = 33. We, thus, preregistered to only discuss events for which we could detect at least medium-sized effects (n ≥ 73) in the main manuscript. As research on event-related changes in sub-Saharan Africa is lacking, we relied on findings from Western countries to derive hypotheses on how personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health change in response to 11 life events that typically occur in emerging adulthood (Table 1). We frame these hypotheses, however, more as tests of generalization than as confirmatory expectations, because of the reasons noted above to expect different associations in sub-Saharan Africa. Other trait-event combinations were tested exploratorily. Based on power calculations, we preregistered a plan to only include events in this manuscript for which we could detect at least medium-sized effects (i.e., n ≥ 73). For marriage and bought a house the final sample size was below this cutoff, which is why results on these events are only presented in the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Event-Related Changes in Personality Traits, Life Satisfaction, and Mental Health: Evidence from a 4-Year Longitudinal Study in sub-Saharan Africa
table.research_questions:
In ALLS data, we can capture the occurrence of 11 life events typically occurring in emerging adulthood: entering a romantic relationship, having first sexual intercourse, getting married, having a child, ending a romantic relationship, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, losing one’s job, getting a driver’s license, moving away from caregiver, buying a house. Although there are several reasons to assume that findings from Western countries do not generalize to sub-Saharan countries, existing research may nonetheless be the best available starting point for the formulation of hypotheses. Based on contemporary meta-analyses (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Mirsu-Paun & Oliver, 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009), we posited 18 hypotheses on how personality traits (agency, communion), life satisfaction, and mental health will change in response to life events (see Table 1).

Table 1: Hypotheses on Event-Related Changes.
Agency: getting married (decrease), having a child (decrease)	
Communion: finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase)
Life satisfaction: entering a romantic relationship (increase), getting married (increase), having a child (increase), ending a romantic relationship (decrease), finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase), losing one's job (decrease)
Mental health: entering a romantic relationship (increase), getting married (increase), having a child (increase), ending a romantic relationship (decrease), finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase), losing one's job (decrease)
	
Note. Hypotheses were based on recent meta-analyses on event-related changes (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Mirsu-Paun & Oliver, 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009). Due to the strong correlation between self-esteem and mental health (Zell & Johansson, 2025), hypotheses for mental health were also based on meta-analytic results for self-esteem. An empty cell indicates that we do not have a directed hypothesis but that we will examine the respective event-outcome link exploratorily. Given the age range of the sample, we expect some events to be relatively rare (e.g., losing a job or buying a house). We decided to nonetheless consider these events in our manuscript to be as comprehensive as possible. However, we will only discuss events for which we can detect at least medium-sized effects in the main manuscript (n ≥ 73)
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer et al., 2024) to investigate event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study conducted in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa. For the present study, we will use data from W1 to W9, which have been collected between January 2022 and April 2026.

ALLS was addressed to emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (aged 18 to 21). Emerging adults were recruited with the help of local research assistants who reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. After providing informed consent, participants completed surveys on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants’ devices, or on paper. These surveys comprised questions on participants’ personality traits, well-being, mental health, demographic characteristics, and life events. All questionnaires were provided in English and assessments took place every 6 months.

More details about the study design of the ALLS can be found in a cohort profile paper (Thalmayer et al., 2024). For the present study, we will use data on personality traits and mental health assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, data on life satisfaction collected at W3 to W9, and data on life events collected at W1 to W9.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: Data from the ALLS have been used in five previous publications (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025; Hofmann et al., 2025; Kura et al., 2025; Rotzinger et al., 2025; Thalmayer et al., 2025). These publications examined, among other things, the structure, correlates, and changes of personality traits in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Furthermore, one study examined event-related changes in personality traits over 1 year using free-text descriptions of important life events (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025). Thus, there are initial insights on event-related personality changes in the ALLS data. However, this study relied on data from two assessment waves only, did not consider changes in other outcomes, examined a different set of life events, and did not investigate non-linear trajectories of traits before and after the event occurrence. Furthermore, there are ongoing theses beyond these publications that examine additional topics using the ALLS data. However, the principal investigator of this study is blind to any insights from these theses. Thus, information relevant to our hypothesis is unknown.
table.data_collection_procedures:
ALLS included participants (a) living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, (b) aged between 18 and 21 years at W1, and (c) speaking at least basic English. 

Participants were recruited from rural villages, towns and urban areas, including from informal settlements. Local research assistants reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. 

The study used a combination of online and paper-pencil methods for data collection. Participants were re-contacted by text, email, or in person via the local research assistants for subsequent assessment waves. This procedure allowed to collect a more representative sample compared to online-only studies as internet access varies across the three countries.
To compensate for early dropout and to include groups and areas underrepresented in initial recruitment, booster samples were added to the study at W3 following the same data collection procedures.
table.sample_size:
Overall, 3’048 individuals took part in W1 of the ALLS. However, 700 individuals could not be reached again at W2 so that a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3. 
For our analyses, we will only use data from assessments where participants passed quality check items (see Data Exclusion section for details). Our final sample size thus still has to be determined.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We expect a final sample size of approximately N = 2,800 individuals. 

Our power to detect significant effects will depend on the number of participants who experienced a certain life event. Power analyses using the R package pwr (Champely, 2006) indicated that we will have a sufficient power (1 – β = 0.80) to detect significant effects (α = .01) with the following sample and effect sizes: 
•	Very small event related changes (d = 0.10): n = 1172
•	Small event-related changes (d = 0.20): n = 296
•	Medium-sized event-related changes (d = 0.41): n = 73
•	Strong event-related changes (d = 0.63): n = 33

Thus, we will interpret findings on life events in context of their base rates and the associated power. We will only discuss events for which we can detect at least medium-sized effects (n ≥ 73) in the main manuscript. Other events will still be analyzed but moved to the supplementary materials.

However, these results should be understood as a rough power estimate only, as the power calculations were based on a different statistical model (dependent sample t-test vs. fixed-effects regressions), because - to the best of our knowledge – power analyses specific to fixed-effect regressions are not implemented in R.
table.stopping_rule: Not applicable as data has already been collected.
table.measured_variables:
Personality traits (assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, W9): 
Agency and communion were assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer et al., 2025). The 45 Items (e.g., “I tend to be calm”) were assessed on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate).

Life satisfaction (assessed at W3 to W9): 
Life satisfaction was assessed with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; Kjell & Diener, 2021): Three items (e.g., “I am satisfied with my life”) were assessed on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Mental health (assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, W9): 
Mental health problems were assessed with the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023). Items (e.g., “I felt scared”) were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 0 (not in the last month/never) to 6 (daily). To ease comparability with the other constructs, we will reverse score this scale so that higher values indicate higher levels of mental health. We will use all items of this questionnaire to create an overall score for mental health except for Substance Abuse Item 2 and Relationship Conflict Item 1 because they have been shown to generalize poorly across countries (Hofmann et al., 2025).

Life events (assessed at W1 to W9): 
We will use two different strategies to identify the occurrence of life events. 

First, some life events were directly assessed with specific questions at each assessment wave: 
-	Moving away from caregivers
-	Getting a driver’s license
-	Finishing education
-	Becoming full-time employed
-	Having first sexual intercourse
-	Buying own house

Second, other life events can be identified by examining changes in demographic variables that were also assessed at each wave: 
-	Entering a romantic relationship: Change in relationship status from “I am not in a relationship” to “I am in a relationship”
-	Marrying: Change in relationship status from “I am not in a relationship” or “I am in a relationship” to “I am married”
-	Ending a romantic relationship: Change in relationship status from “I am in a relationship” or “I am married” to “I am not in a relationship”
-	Losing one’s job: Change in employment status from any kind of paid work to “unemployed”
-	Having a child: Increase in the number of own children
table.indices: We will reverse code items of all multi-item measures (e.g., life satisfaction, personality traits) if necessary and calculate a mean score for the analyses. We will calculate mean scores even if not all items of a scale have been answered. Furthermore, as described above, we will identify the occurrence of life events and code mental health so that higher values mean higher mental health.
table.statistical_tests:
We will use R and R packages plm (Croissant & Millo, 2008), multicomp (Hothorn et al., 2002), tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019). Our analyses will comprise three steps.

Step 1: Identification of Event Groups and Control Groups
In a first step, we will identify the occurrence of the eleven life events of interest from W2 onward (entering a romantic relationship, having first sexual intercourse, getting married, having a child, ending a romantic relationship, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, losing one’s job, getting a driver’s license, moving away from caregiver, buying a house). That is, we cannot consider event occurrence at W1. For example, if participants reported that they already moved out from home at W1, we cannot consider this event for this person because we lack information on the timing of the event occurrence. 

Furthermore, for all life events, we will consider the first event occurrence only. For example, if a participant reported multiple marriages, we will focus on the first marriage in our analyses. Similarly, if participants reported that they moved out of home at multiple assessments, we will consider its first mention. 

Additionally, we will create control groups for each life event comprising individuals who did not experience the event across the study period but could in principle have experienced it. This control group will allow for a more precise estimation of age-graded trajectories in our analyses. Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see Krämer et al., 2025, for a similar approach): 
- Ending a romantic relationship: Individuals who are in a romantic relationship or marriage at some point during the study period 
- Losing one’s job: Individuals who are employed at some point during the study period
- Moving away from caregiver, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, having first sexual intercourse, buying own house: Individuals who did not yet experience this event at W1
- Entering romantic relationship, marrying, having a child: No specific criterion for control group

We will z-standardize all outcome variables within the overall sample (i.e., across groups). 

Step 2: Fixed-Effects Regression Models
As a second step, we will then use fixed-effect regressions to examine event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences (Allison, 2009). This approach thus automatically controls for all time-invariant confounders, such as country, gender, childhood characteristics. It is comparable to person-mean centering in multilevel regression but relies on fewer statistical assumptions (McNeish & Kelley, 2019). Fixed-effect regressions are thus a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Krämer et al., 2025).

We will run one model for each event-outcome combination (11 x 4 = 44 models). Personality trait scores, life satisfaction, and mental health for person i at time point t will serve as dependent variable (Traitit). Time from and to event occurrence will serve as predictors. Specifically, we will include five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables to capture non-linear event-related changes in response to life events: 
- D-2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D-1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D+1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year after the occurrence of the target event
- D+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) after the occurrence of the target event
- D>+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place more than 2 years after the occurrence of the target event

Using these dummies allows us to estimate within-person changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health, without assuming a specific functional form. Furthermore, it allows us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025). 

Finally, to control for normative changes in our outcomes of interest, we will include 〖Age〗_it and 〖Age〗_it^2 as predictors in our models. 
Participants belonging to the control group will receive a zero on all event-related dummies. These participants will thus only contribute to the estimation of the intercept and age-related changes.

An example model equation reads as follows: 
〖Trait〗_it=α_i+β_1∙D_(〖-2Y〗_it )+β_2∙D_(〖-1Y〗_it )+β_3∙D_(〖+1Y〗_it )+β_4∙D_(〖+2Y〗_it )+β_5∙D_(〖>+2Y〗_it )+β_6∙〖Age〗_it+β_7∙〖Age〗_it^2+ε_it

α_i represents the person-specific fixed effects that account for stable between-person differences. β_1 to β_5 capture event-related changes before and after the event occurrence, whereas β_6 to β_7 capture age-related changes. We will estimate the significance of these effects using cluster-robust standard errors (Arellano method with small sample correction). To evaluate our hypotheses, we will examine the direction and statistical significance of β_1 to β_5. An effect will be interpreted as being in line with our hypotheses, if we observe significant changes in the expected direction for any event-related dummy. Furthermore, we will compare the size of event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

As a supplementary analysis, we will examine linear contrast across event-related dummies to examine changes from specific pre-event to specific post-event assessments. These linear contrasts will, for example, inform us whether there are significant changes from assessments 1 year before the event occurrence to 1 year after the event occurrence.

Step 3: Robustness Check
As a robustness check, we will repeat the analyses from Step 2 using differently specified event-related dummies. Specifically, we will run a simplified model with just two event-related dummies: 
- DPre = 1: All assessments that take place up to 2 years prior to the occurrence of the target event
- DPost = 1: All assessments that take place after the occurrence of the target event

This simplified model combines all assessments taking place up to 2 years before the event occurrence in one dummy and all assessment taking place after the event occurrence in another dummy. It thus increases statistical power to identify significant effects. The linear contrast DPre – DPost = 0 allows us to examine whether there are event-related changes from pre- to post-event assessments. This contrast can thus be used compare effect sizes to effect sizes from meta-analyses using simple pre-post comparisons (Bühler et al., 2024).
table.transformations: We will z-standardize agency, communion, life satisfaction, mental health in the overall sample.
table.inference_criteria: Each event-outcome combination tests a different hypothesis so that we will not correct for the number of models. However, within each event-outcome combination, we will have five statistical tests according to the five regression coefficients (β_1 to β_5) to evaluate each hypothesis. Thus, we will use an adjusted level of significance of α = .05/5 = .01 for our analyses. Furthermore, we will put emphasis on effect sizes in the interpretation of our findings.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude data from assessment waves where participants failed the attention check items. Specifically, in line with recommendations of the ALLS investigators, we will exclude participants if they failed all attention check items at W1 (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items; “for this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate”). At other waves, where improved quality check items were used, we will exclude participants who failed at least one attention check item (e.g., “Hello, are you still paying attention? Which of the following is an animal? – House, tree, plane, cat, book”).
table.missing_data_handling: All cases with data for the dependent and independent variables will be included in the analyses. Even if participants contributed to only one assessment wave their data can still be used for the estimation of intercepts and age-effects.
table.exploratory_analyses: Although recent research suggests that a single higher-order factor is appropriate to capture mental health in sub-Saharan Africa (Hofmann et al., 2025), looking at lower-order aspects of mental health may be interesting to get more nuanced insights into the links between life events and different kinds of mental health problems (e.g., dysregulated sleep, negative affect, or substance use). Therefore, we will repeat the above-described analyses using depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep difficulties, life stress, anger, harmful substance use, interpersonal conflict, and psychosis as lower-level aspects of mental health (excluding the same items mentioned above).

table.title: Event-Related Changes in Personality Traits, Life Satisfaction, and Mental Health: Evidence from a 4-Year Longitudinal Study in sub-Saharan Africa
table.research_questions:
In ALLS data, we can capture the occurrence of 11 life events typically occurring in emerging adulthood: entering a romantic relationship, having first sexual intercourse, getting married, having a child, ending a romantic relationship, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, losing one’s job, getting a driver’s license, moving away from caregiver, buying a house. Although there are several reasons to assume that findings from Western countries do not generalize to sub-Saharan countries, existing research may nonetheless be the best available starting point for the formulation of hypotheses. Based on contemporary meta-analyses (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Mirsu-Paun & Oliver, 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009), we posited 18 hypotheses on how personality traits (agency, communion), life satisfaction, and mental health will change in response to life events (see Table 1).

Table 1: Hypotheses on Event-Related Changes.
Agency: getting married (decrease), having a child (decrease)	
Communion: finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase)
Life satisfaction: entering a romantic relationship (increase), getting married (increase), having a child (increase), ending a romantic relationship (decrease), finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase), losing one's job (decrease)
Mental health: entering a romantic relationship (increase), getting married (increase), having a child (increase), ending a romantic relationship (decrease), finishing education (increase), becoming full-time employed (increase), losing one's job (decrease)
	
Note. Hypotheses were based on recent meta-analyses on event-related changes (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Mirsu-Paun & Oliver, 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009). Due to the strong correlation between self-esteem and mental health (Zell & Johansson, 2025), hypotheses for mental health were also based on meta-analytic results for self-esteem. An empty cell indicates that we do not have a directed hypothesis but that we will examine the respective event-outcome link exploratorily. Given the age range of the sample, we expect some events to be relatively rare (e.g., losing a job or buying a house). We decided to nonetheless consider these events in our manuscript to be as comprehensive as possible. However, we will only discuss events for which we can detect at least medium-sized effects in the main manuscript (n ≥ 73)
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer et al., 2024) to investigate event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study conducted in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa. For the present study, we will use data from W1 to W9, which have been collected between January 2022 and April 2026.

ALLS was addressed to emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (aged 18 to 21). Emerging adults were recruited with the help of local research assistants who reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. After providing informed consent, participants completed surveys on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants’ devices, or on paper. These surveys comprised questions on participants’ personality traits, well-being, mental health, demographic characteristics, and life events. All questionnaires were provided in English and assessments took place every 6 months.

More details about the study design of the ALLS can be found in a cohort profile paper (Thalmayer et al., 2024). For the present study, we will use data on personality traits and mental health assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, data on life satisfaction collected at W3 to W9, and data on life events collected at W1 to W9.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation: Data from the ALLS have been used in five previous publications (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025; Hofmann et al., 2025; Kura et al., 2025; Rotzinger et al., 2025; Thalmayer et al., 2025). These publications examined, among other things, the structure, correlates, and changes of personality traits in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Furthermore, one study examined event-related changes in personality traits over 1 year using free-text descriptions of important life events (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025). Thus, there are initial insights on event-related personality changes in the ALLS data. However, this study relied on data from two assessment waves only, did not consider changes in other outcomes, examined a different set of life events, and did not investigate non-linear trajectories of traits before and after the event occurrence. Furthermore, there are ongoing theses beyond these publications that examine additional topics using the ALLS data. However, the principal investigator of this study is blind to any insights from these theses. Thus, information relevant to our hypothesis is unknown.
table.data_collection_procedures:
ALLS included participants (a) living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, (b) aged between 18 and 21 years at W1, and (c) speaking at least basic English. 

Participants were recruited from rural villages, towns and urban areas, including from informal settlements. Local research assistants reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools. 

The study used a combination of online and paper-pencil methods for data collection. Participants were re-contacted by text, email, or in person via the local research assistants for subsequent assessment waves. This procedure allowed to collect a more representative sample compared to online-only studies as internet access varies across the three countries.
To compensate for early dropout and to include groups and areas underrepresented in initial recruitment, booster samples were added to the study at W3 following the same data collection procedures.
table.sample_size:
Overall, 3’048 individuals took part in W1 of the ALLS. However, 700 individuals could not be reached again at W2 so that a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3. 
For our analyses, we will only use data from assessments where participants passed quality check items (see Data Exclusion section for details). Our final sample size thus still has to be determined.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We expect a final sample size of approximately N = 2,800 individuals. 

Our power to detect significant effects will depend on the number of participants who experienced a certain life event. Power analyses using the R package pwr (Champely, 2006) indicated that we will have a sufficient power (1 – β = 0.80) to detect significant effects (α = .01) with the following sample and effect sizes: 
•	Very small event related changes (d = 0.10): n = 1172
•	Small event-related changes (d = 0.20): n = 296
•	Medium-sized event-related changes (d = 0.41): n = 73
•	Strong event-related changes (d = 0.63): n = 33

Thus, we will interpret findings on life events in context of their base rates and the associated power. We will only discuss events for which we can detect at least medium-sized effects (n ≥ 73) in the main manuscript. Other events will still be analyzed but moved to the supplementary materials.

However, these results should be understood as a rough power estimate only, as the power calculations were based on a different statistical model (dependent sample t-test vs. fixed-effects regressions), because - to the best of our knowledge – power analyses specific to fixed-effect regressions are not implemented in R.
table.stopping_rule: Not applicable as data has already been collected.
table.measured_variables:
Personality traits (assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, W9): 
Agency and communion were assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer et al., 2025). The 45 Items (e.g., “I tend to be calm”) were assessed on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate).

Life satisfaction (assessed at W3 to W9): 
Life satisfaction was assessed with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; Kjell & Diener, 2021): Three items (e.g., “I am satisfied with my life”) were assessed on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Mental health (assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, W9): 
Mental health problems were assessed with the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023). Items (e.g., “I felt scared”) were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 0 (not in the last month/never) to 6 (daily). To ease comparability with the other constructs, we will reverse score this scale so that higher values indicate higher levels of mental health. We will use all items of this questionnaire to create an overall score for mental health except for Substance Abuse Item 2 and Relationship Conflict Item 1 because they have been shown to generalize poorly across countries (Hofmann et al., 2025).

Life events (assessed at W1 to W9): 
We will use two different strategies to identify the occurrence of life events. 

First, some life events were directly assessed with specific questions at each assessment wave: 
-	Moving away from caregivers
-	Getting a driver’s license
-	Finishing education
-	Becoming full-time employed
-	Having first sexual intercourse
-	Buying own house

Second, other life events can be identified by examining changes in demographic variables that were also assessed at each wave: 
-	Entering a romantic relationship: Change in relationship status from “I am not in a relationship” to “I am in a relationship”
-	Marrying: Change in relationship status from “I am not in a relationship” or “I am in a relationship” to “I am married”
-	Ending a romantic relationship: Change in relationship status from “I am in a relationship” or “I am married” to “I am not in a relationship”
-	Losing one’s job: Change in employment status from any kind of paid work to “unemployed”
-	Having a child: Increase in the number of own children
table.indices: We will reverse code items of all multi-item measures (e.g., life satisfaction, personality traits) if necessary and calculate a mean score for the analyses. We will calculate mean scores even if not all items of a scale have been answered. Furthermore, as described above, we will identify the occurrence of life events and code mental health so that higher values mean higher mental health.
table.statistical_tests:
We will use R and R packages plm (Croissant & Millo, 2008), multicomp (Hothorn et al., 2002), tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019). Our analyses will comprise three steps.

Step 1: Identification of Event Groups and Control Groups
In a first step, we will identify the occurrence of the eleven life events of interest from W2 onward (entering a romantic relationship, having first sexual intercourse, getting married, having a child, ending a romantic relationship, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, losing one’s job, getting a driver’s license, moving away from caregiver, buying a house). That is, we cannot consider event occurrence at W1. For example, if participants reported that they already moved out from home at W1, we cannot consider this event for this person because we lack information on the timing of the event occurrence. 

Furthermore, for all life events, we will consider the first event occurrence only. For example, if a participant reported multiple marriages, we will focus on the first marriage in our analyses. Similarly, if participants reported that they moved out of home at multiple assessments, we will consider its first mention. 

Additionally, we will create control groups for each life event comprising individuals who did not experience the event across the study period but could in principle have experienced it. This control group will allow for a more precise estimation of age-graded trajectories in our analyses. Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see Krämer et al., 2025, for a similar approach): 
- Ending a romantic relationship: Individuals who are in a romantic relationship or marriage at some point during the study period 
- Losing one’s job: Individuals who are employed at some point during the study period
- Moving away from caregiver, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, having first sexual intercourse, buying own house: Individuals who did not yet experience this event at W1
- Entering romantic relationship, marrying, having a child: No specific criterion for control group

We will z-standardize all outcome variables within the overall sample (i.e., across groups). 

Step 2: Fixed-Effects Regression Models
As a second step, we will then use fixed-effect regressions to examine event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences (Allison, 2009). This approach thus automatically controls for all time-invariant confounders, such as country, gender, childhood characteristics. It is comparable to person-mean centering in multilevel regression but relies on fewer statistical assumptions (McNeish & Kelley, 2019). Fixed-effect regressions are thus a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Krämer et al., 2025).

We will run one model for each event-outcome combination (11 x 4 = 44 models). Personality trait scores, life satisfaction, and mental health for person i at time point t will serve as dependent variable (Traitit). Time from and to event occurrence will serve as predictors. Specifically, we will include five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables to capture non-linear event-related changes in response to life events: 
- D-2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D-1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D+1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year after the occurrence of the target event
- D+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) after the occurrence of the target event
- D>+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place more than 2 years after the occurrence of the target event

Using these dummies allows us to estimate within-person changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health, without assuming a specific functional form. Furthermore, it allows us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025). 

Finally, to control for normative changes in our outcomes of interest, we will include 〖Age〗_it and 〖Age〗_it^2 as predictors in our models. 
Participants belonging to the control group will receive a zero on all event-related dummies. These participants will thus only contribute to the estimation of the intercept and age-related changes.

An example model equation reads as follows: 
〖Trait〗_it=α_i+β_1∙D_(〖-2Y〗_it )+β_2∙D_(〖-1Y〗_it )+β_3∙D_(〖+1Y〗_it )+β_4∙D_(〖+2Y〗_it )+β_5∙D_(〖>+2Y〗_it )+β_6∙〖Age〗_it+β_7∙〖Age〗_it^2+ε_it

α_i represents the person-specific fixed effects that account for stable between-person differences. β_1 to β_5 capture event-related changes before and after the event occurrence, whereas β_6 to β_7 capture age-related changes. We will estimate the significance of these effects using cluster-robust standard errors (Arellano method with small sample correction). To evaluate our hypotheses, we will examine the direction and statistical significance of β_1 to β_5. An effect will be interpreted as being in line with our hypotheses, if we observe significant changes in the expected direction for any event-related dummy. Furthermore, we will compare the size of event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

As a supplementary analysis, we will examine linear contrast across event-related dummies to examine changes from specific pre-event to specific post-event assessments. These linear contrasts will, for example, inform us whether there are significant changes from assessments 1 year before the event occurrence to 1 year after the event occurrence.

Step 3: Robustness Check
As a robustness check, we will repeat the analyses from Step 2 using differently specified event-related dummies. Specifically, we will run a simplified model with just two event-related dummies: 
- DPre = 1: All assessments that take place up to 2 years prior to the occurrence of the target event
- DPost = 1: All assessments that take place after the occurrence of the target event

This simplified model combines all assessments taking place up to 2 years before the event occurrence in one dummy and all assessment taking place after the event occurrence in another dummy. It thus increases statistical power to identify significant effects. The linear contrast DPre – DPost = 0 allows us to examine whether there are event-related changes from pre- to post-event assessments. This contrast can thus be used compare effect sizes to effect sizes from meta-analyses using simple pre-post comparisons (Bühler et al., 2024).
table.transformations: We will z-standardize agency, communion, life satisfaction, mental health in the overall sample.
table.inference_criteria: Each event-outcome combination tests a different hypothesis so that we will not correct for the number of models. However, within each event-outcome combination, we will have five statistical tests according to the five regression coefficients (β_1 to β_5) to evaluate each hypothesis. Thus, we will use an adjusted level of significance of α = .05/5 = .01 for our analyses. Furthermore, we will put emphasis on effect sizes in the interpretation of our findings.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude data from assessment waves where participants failed the attention check items. Specifically, in line with recommendations of the ALLS investigators, we will exclude participants if they failed all attention check items at W1 (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items; “for this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate”). At other waves, where improved quality check items were used, we will exclude participants who failed at least one attention check item (e.g., “Hello, are you still paying attention? Which of the following is an animal? – House, tree, plane, cat, book”).
table.missing_data_handling: All cases with data for the dependent and independent variables will be included in the analyses. Even if participants contributed to only one assessment wave their data can still be used for the estimation of intercepts and age-effects.
table.exploratory_analyses: Although recent research suggests that a single higher-order factor is appropriate to capture mental health in sub-Saharan Africa (Hofmann et al., 2025), looking at lower-order aspects of mental health may be interesting to get more nuanced insights into the links between life events and different kinds of mental health problems (e.g., dysregulated sleep, negative affect, or substance use). Therefore, we will repeat the above-described analyses using depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep difficulties, life stress, anger, harmful substance use, interpersonal conflict, and psychosis as lower-level aspects of mental health (excluding the same items mentioned above).

Similarly, if participants reported that they moved out of home at multiple assessments, we will consider its first mention.

Additionally, we will create control groups for each life event comprising individuals who did not experience the event across the study period but could in principle have experienced it. This control group will allow for a more precise estimation of age-graded trajectories in our analyses. Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see Krämer et al., 2025, for a similar approach):
- Ending a romantic relationship: Individuals who are in a romantic relationship or marriage at some point during the study period
- Losing one’s job: Individuals who are employed at some point during the study period
- Moving away from caregiver, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, having first sexual intercourse, buying own house: Individuals who did not yet experience this event at W1
- Entering romantic relationship, marrying, having a child: No specific criterion for control group

We will z-standardize all outcome variables within the overall sample (i.e., across groups).

Step 2: Fixed-Effects Regression Models
As a second step, we will then use fixed-effect regressions to examine event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences (Allison, 2009). This approach thus automatically controls for all time-invariant confounders, such as country, gender, childhood characteristics. It is comparable to person-mean centering in multilevel regression but relies on fewer statistical assumptions (McNeish & Kelley, 2019). Fixed-effect regressions are thus a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Krämer et al., 2025).

We will run one model for each event-outcome combination (11 x 4 = 44 models). Personality trait scores, life satisfaction, and mental health for person i at time point t will serve as dependent variable (Traitit). Time from and to event occurrence will serve as predictors. Specifically, we will include five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables to capture non-linear event-related changes in response to life events:
- D-2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D-1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D+1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year after the occurrence of the target event
- D+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) after the occurrence of the target event
- D>+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place more than 2 years after the occurrence of the target event

Using these dummies allows us to estimate within-person changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health, without assuming a specific functional form. Furthermore, it allows us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

Finally, to control for normative changes in our outcomes of interest, we will include 〖Age〗_it and 〖Age〗_it^2 as predictors in our models.
Participants belonging to the control group will receive a zero on all event-related dummies. These participants will thus only contribute to the estimation of the intercept and age-related changes.

An example model equation reads as follows:
〖Trait〗_it=α_i+β_1∙D_(〖-2Y〗_it )+β_2∙D_(〖-1Y〗_it )+β_3∙D_(〖+1Y〗_it )+β_4∙D_(〖+2Y〗_it )+β_5∙D_(〖>+2Y〗_it )+β_6∙〖Age〗_it+β_7∙〖Age〗_it^2+ε_it

α_i represents the person-specific fixed effects that account for stable between-person differences. β_1 to β_5 capture event-related changes before and after the event occurrence, whereas β_6 to β_7 capture age-related changes. We will estimate the significance of these effects using cluster-robust standard errors (Arellano method with small sample correction). To evaluate our hypotheses, we will examine the direction and statistical significance of β_1 to β_5. An effect will be interpreted as being in line with our hypotheses, if we observe significant changes in the expected direction for any event-related dummy. Furthermore, we will compare the size of event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

As a supplementary analysis, we will examine linear contrast across event-related dummies to examine changes from specific pre-event to specific post-event assessments. These linear contrasts will, for example, inform us whether there are significant changes from assessments 1 year before the event occurrence to 1 year after the event occurrence.

Step 3: Robustness Check
As a robustness check, we will repeat the analyses from Step 2 using differently specified event-related dummies. Specifically, we will run a simplified model with just two event-related dummies:
- DPre = 1: All assessments that take place up to 2 years prior to the occurrence of the target event
- DPost = 1: All assessments that take place after the occurrence of the target event

This simplified model combines all assessments taking place up to 2 years before the event occurrence in one dummy and all assessment taking place after the event occurrence in another dummy. It thus increases statistical power to identify significant effects. The linear contrast DPre – DPost = 0 allows us to examine whether there are event-related changes from pre- to post-event assessments. Step 1: Identification of Event Groups and Control Groups
In a first step, we will identify the occurrence of the eleven life events of interest from W2 onward (entering a romantic relationship, having first sexual intercourse, getting married, having a child, ending a romantic relationship, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, losing one’s job, getting a driver’s license, moving away from caregiver, buying a house). That is, we cannot consider event occurrence at W1. For example, if participants reported that they already moved out from home at W1, we cannot consider this event for this person because we lack information on the timing of the event occurrence.

Furthermore, for all life events, we will consider the first event occurrence only. For example, if a participant reported multiple marriages, we will focus on the first marriage in our analyses. Similarly, if participants reported that they moved out of home at multiple assessments, we will consider its first mention.

Additionally, we will create control groups for each life event comprising individuals who did not experience the event across the study period but could in principle have experienced it. This control group will allow for a more precise estimation of age-graded trajectories in our analyses. Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see Krämer et al., 2025, for a similar approach):
- Ending a romantic relationship: Individuals who are in a romantic relationship or marriage at some point during the study period
- Losing one’s job: Individuals who are employed at some point during the study period
- Moving away from caregiver, finishing education, becoming full-time employed, having first sexual intercourse, buying own house: Individuals who did not yet experience this event at W1
- Entering romantic relationship, marrying, having a child: No specific criterion for control group

We will z-standardize all outcome variables within the overall sample (i.e., across groups).

Step 2: Fixed-Effects Regression Models
As a second step, we will then use fixed-effect regressions to examine event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences (Allison, 2009). This approach thus automatically controls for all time-invariant confounders, such as country, gender, childhood characteristics. It is comparable to person-mean centering in multilevel regression but relies on fewer statistical assumptions (McNeish & Kelley, 2019). Fixed-effect regressions are thus a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025; Krämer et al., 2025).

We will run one model for each event-outcome combination (11 x 4 = 44 models). Personality trait scores, life satisfaction, and mental health for person i at time point t will serve as dependent variable (Traitit). Time from and to event occurrence will serve as predictors. Specifically, we will include five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables to capture non-linear event-related changes in response to life events:
- D-2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D-1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year prior to the occurrence of the target event
- D+1Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 1 year after the occurrence of the target event
- D+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place up to 2 years (but more than 1 year) after the occurrence of the target event
- D>+2Y = 1: Assessments that take place more than 2 years after the occurrence of the target event

Using these dummies allows us to estimate within-person changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health, without assuming a specific functional form. Furthermore, it allows us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

Finally, to control for normative changes in our outcomes of interest, we will include 〖Age〗_it and 〖Age〗_it^2 as predictors in our models.
Participants belonging to the control group will receive a zero on all event-related dummies. These participants will thus only contribute to the estimation of the intercept and age-related changes.

An example model equation reads as follows:
〖Trait〗_it=α_i+β_1∙D_(〖-2Y〗_it )+β_2∙D_(〖-1Y〗_it )+β_3∙D_(〖+1Y〗_it )+β_4∙D_(〖+2Y〗_it )+β_5∙D_(〖>+2Y〗_it )+β_6∙〖Age〗_it+β_7∙〖Age〗_it^2+ε_it

α_i represents the person-specific fixed effects that account for stable between-person differences. β_1 to β_5 capture event-related changes before and after the event occurrence, whereas β_6 to β_7 capture age-related changes. We will estimate the significance of these effects using cluster-robust standard errors (Arellano method with small sample correction). To evaluate our hypotheses, we will examine the direction and statistical significance of β_1 to β_5. An effect will be interpreted as being in line with our hypotheses, if we observe significant changes in the expected direction for any event-related dummy. Furthermore, we will compare the size of event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2025).

As a supplementary analysis, we will examine linear contrast across event-related dummies to examine changes from specific pre-event to specific post-event assessments. These linear contrasts will, for example, inform us whether there are significant changes from assessments 1 year before the event occurrence to 1 year after the event occurrence.

Step 3: Robustness Check
As a robustness check, we will repeat the analyses from Step 2 using differently specified event-related dummies. Specifically, we will run a simplified model with just two event-related dummies:
- DPre = 1: All assessments that take place up to 2 years prior to the occurrence of the target event
- DPost = 1: All assessments that take place after the occurrence of the target event

This simplified model combines all assessments taking place up to 2 years before the event occurrence in one dummy and all assessment taking place after the event occurrence in another dummy. It thus increases statistical power to identify significant effects. The linear contrast DPre – DPost = 0 allows us to examine whether there are event-related changes from pre- to post-event assessments. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1792 columns across 1 data file.
#### Issues Identified

34 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethics: Data collection of the ALLS was approved by the ethics committee of the five partner universities and at the national levels in Kenya and Namibia.
live_data_statements: Participants were recruited with the help of local research assistants who reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools.
After providing informed consent, participants completed surveys on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants' devices, or on paper.
Assessment waves (henceforward called W1 to W9) took place every 6 months, when participants were re-contacted by text, email, or in person via the local research assistants.
At W1, participants were on average 18.30 years old (SD = 0.72).
Participants were approximately equally distributed across the three countries (Kenya: 34%, Namibia: 33%, South Africa: 33%), 56% of the sample were female, and 67% had high school level education.
These samples sizes of the event groups refer to "robust event occurrences", meaning that participants had to report a respective life change at two consecutive assessments.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:4, File = c("01 Data Preparation.R", 
"02 Data Preparation_RobustEvents.R", "Supplement_Events_v4.R", 
"Supplement_Events_v4.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "01 Data Preparation.R", 
"02 Data Preparation_RobustEvents.R, 01 Data Preparation.R"), 
    Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "dependency", "dependency"
    )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 2 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `Supplement_Events_v4.Rmd` (data_full_robust.RData, data_events_robust.RData). 2 files were written in another folder than where the script looked, so before that run we copied them there: `data_full_robust.RData` to `Data/data_full_robust.RData` for `Supplement_Events_v4.Rmd`; `data_events_robust.RData` to `Data/data_events_robust.RData` for `Supplement_Events_v4.Rmd`. The scripts assume they all run from one folder; saying which, or building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), solves this. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("01 Data Preparation.R", "02 Data Preparation_RobustEvents.R", 
"Supplement_Events_v4.R", "Supplement_Events_v4.Rmd"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", 
"ran_ok", "errored", "errored"), Detail = c("", "", "undefined_variable", 
"runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(26.6, 25.6, 5, 41.7)), row.names = c(NA, 
-4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplement_Events_v4.R", "Missing variable" = "data_full", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: 02 Data Preparation_RobustEvents.R, 01 Data Preparation.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("02 Data Preparation_RobustEvents.R", 
"01 Data Preparation.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(2L, 2L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplement_Events_v4.R", "library() calls added" = "library(tidyverse), library(writexl), library(readxl), library(papaja), library(kableExtra), library(cowplot), library(psych), library(ggridges), library(ggiraph), library(plm), library(multcomp)"), row.names = "Supplement_Events_v4.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: Life events like entering a romantic relationship or losing a job have been found to predict changes in personality traits and well-being.
However, findings on event-related changes stem almost exclusively from Western countries.

Here, we address this limitation by examining event-related changes in agency, communion, life satisfaction, and mental health among young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (N = 3,928).

A finding that converged with prior meta-analyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency whereas event-related changes in other events diverged substantially from findings in Western samples.
For example, finishing education or getting a driver's license predicted decreases in agency and communion.
Furthermore, having first sexual intercourse was associated with decreases in mental health.
Future cross-cultural research is needed to test potential explanations for why event-related changes differ across cultural contexts.

Emerging adulthood is a pivotal developmental phase with important life transitions and first-time experiences of significant events, such as entering the workforce or graduation (Arnett, 2007; Hutteman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Emerging adulthood is a pivotal developmental phase with important life transitions and first-time experiences of significant events, such as entering the workforce or graduation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arnett, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hutteman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These events have been theorized to catalyze changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health in emerging adulthood and beyond (Bleidorn et al., 2018; Cohen et al., 2019; Lucas, 2007).
text.formatted: These events have been theorized to catalyze changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health in emerging adulthood and beyond <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bleidorn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cohen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lucas, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Becoming an employee may, for example, trigger increases in communion-related traits because it requires individuals to be polite, industrious, and friendly (Roberts & Nickel, 2017).
text.formatted: Becoming an employee may, for example, trigger increases in communion-related traits because it requires individuals to be polite, industrious, and friendly <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, this event may trigger increases in people's mental health and life satisfaction because it increases resources and evokes positive emotions (Headey, 2010; Luhmann & Intelisano, 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, this event may trigger increases in people's mental health and life satisfaction because it increases resources and evokes positive emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Headey, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Luhmann & Intelisano, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Comprehensive meta-analyses support the relevance of life events for triggering psychological change.

For example, entering the workforce has been linked to increases in life satisfaction and conscientiousness, whereas unemployment has been found to predict increases in depression and anxiety (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026; Luhmann et al., 2012; March-Llanes et al., 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009).
text.formatted: For example, entering the workforce has been linked to increases in life satisfaction and conscientiousness, whereas unemployment has been found to predict increases in depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bühler et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Luhmann et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">March-Llanes et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Paul & Moser, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence on the effects of life events stems almost exclusively from Western countries.
For example, a recent meta-analysis on event-related personality changes did not include any studies from Africa (Bühler et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, a recent meta-analysis on event-related personality changes did not include any studies from Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bühler et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, four recent meta-analyses on event-related changes in mental health, together comprised only one study conducted in Africa (Haehner et al., 2024; Hühne et al., 2025; March-Llanes et al., 2017; Paul & Moser, 2009).
text.formatted: Likewise, four recent meta-analyses on event-related changes in mental health, together comprised only one study conducted in Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Haehner et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hühne et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">March-Llanes et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Paul & Moser, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, there is a strong need to diversify research on the effects of life events.
A thorough examination of event-related changes in samples from sub-Saharan Africa could advance psychological research in multiple ways.

First, as most psychological phenomena are influenced by cultural context, it may be a fallacy to assume that findings on event-related changes from Western countries generalize to other cultural contexts (Henrich et al., 2010; Kitayama & Salvador, 2024).
text.formatted: First, as most psychological phenomena are influenced by cultural context, it may be a fallacy to assume that findings on event-related changes from Western countries generalize to other cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Henrich et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kitayama & Salvador, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, examining event-related changes in African countries may help advance theory, because available models provide limited insights into how cultural context influences changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health (Bleidorn, 2024; Thalmayer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Second, examining event-related changes in African countries may help advance theory, because available models provide limited insights into how cultural context influences changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Thalmayer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Third, this topic has applied relevance, as understanding the conditions under which emerging adults in this region thrive or struggle can inform contextually-appropriate interventions.
This is particularly important because sub-Saharan Africa is home to more of the world's population than all Western countries combined (United Nations, 2025).
text.formatted: This is particularly important because sub-Saharan Africa is home to more of the world's population than all Western countries combined <ref type="bibr">(United Nations, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While some mechanisms theorized to drive changes in personality traits, well-being, and mental health may act similarly across cultural contexts (e.g., Wrzus & Roberts, 2017), there are also good reasons to assume that findings from Western countries will not generalize to African contexts.
text.formatted: While some mechanisms theorized to drive changes in personality traits, well-being, and mental health may act similarly across cultural contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Wrzus & Roberts, 2017)</ref>, there are also good reasons to assume that findings from Western countries will not generalize to African contexts.

text.text: Existing research has, for instance, shown that the structure of both personality traits and psychopathology differs across cultural contexts (Laher & Cheung, 2022).
text.formatted: Existing research has, for instance, shown that the structure of both personality traits and psychopathology differs across cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Laher & Cheung, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While most research in Western countries relies on Big Five personality traits, the Cross-Cultural Big Two personality traits, agency (i.e., tendency to be sociable, surgent, confident, and fearless) and communion (i.e., tendency to be warm, respectful, industrious, and eventempered), appear to work better in African countries and for cross-cultural comparisons (Thalmayer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: While most research in Western countries relies on Big Five personality traits, the Cross-Cultural Big Two personality traits, agency (i.e., tendency to be sociable, surgent, confident, and fearless) and communion (i.e., tendency to be warm, respectful, industrious, and eventempered), appear to work better in African countries and for cross-cultural comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Thalmayer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a unidimensional model to capture mental health tends to fit better in sub-Saharan Africa than an internalizing-externalizing distinction (Hofmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, a unidimensional model to capture mental health tends to fit better in sub-Saharan Africa than an internalizing-externalizing distinction <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hofmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, there are differences in social roles and economic resources that could shape how personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health change in response to life events (Naudé & Esau, 2024; Uugwanga et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Furthermore, there are differences in social roles and economic resources that could shape how personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health change in response to life events <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Naudé & Esau, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Uugwanga et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa often face limited resources, high unemployment rates, and the need to financially support their families, potentially shifting the meaning of life events such as finishing education or starting full-time employment (Naudé & Esau, 2024; Theron, 2013; Theron et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For example, emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa often face limited resources, high unemployment rates, and the need to financially support their families, potentially shifting the meaning of life events such as finishing education or starting full-time employment <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Naudé & Esau, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Theron, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Theron et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Aligned with this idea, there is initial evidence that education-related events are of particular relevance for emerging adults from sub-Saharan Africa and that the effects of some life events on personality are even stronger than in Western countries (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Aligned with this idea, there is initial evidence that education-related events are of particular relevance for emerging adults from sub-Saharan Africa and that the effects of some life events on personality are even stronger than in Western countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: With the present study, we aim to contribute to a better understanding of the crosscultural generalizability of the effects of life events.

We use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer et al., 2024)-a multi-year longitudinal study of more than 3,000 emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa-to examine changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health in response to important life events.
text.formatted: We use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Thalmayer et al., 2024</ref>)-a multi-year longitudinal study of more than 3,000 emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa-to examine changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health in response to important life events.

text.text: As research on event-related changes in sub-Saharan Africa is lacking, we relied on findings from Western countries to derive hypotheses on how personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health change in response to 11 life events that typically occur in emerging adulthood (Table 1).
text.formatted: As research on event-related changes in sub-Saharan Africa is lacking, we relied on findings from Western countries to derive hypotheses on how personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health change in response to 11 life events that typically occur in emerging adulthood (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We frame these hypotheses, however, more as tests of generalization than as confirmatory expectations, because of the reasons noted above to expect different associations in sub-Saharan Africa.
Other trait-event combinations were tested exploratorily.
Based on power calculations, we preregistered a plan to only include events in this manuscript for which we could detect at least medium-sized effects (i.e., n ≥ 73).

For marriage and bought a house the final sample size was below this cutoff, which is why results on these events are only presented in the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915).
