text.text: ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study of emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (Thalmayer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study of emerging adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Thalmayer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were recruited with the help of local research assistants who reached out to eligible individuals via local networks, community events, and high schools.
After providing informed consent, participants completed surveys on electronic devices carried by the research assistants, via links sent to participants' devices, or on paper.
These surveys comprised questions on participants' personality traits, well-being, mental health, demographic characteristics, and life events.
All questionnaires were provided in English.
Assessment waves (henceforward called W1 to W9) took place every 6 months, when participants were re-contacted by text, email, or in person via the local research assistants.
This procedure allowed collecting a more representative sample compared to online-only studies.

For the present study, we used data on personality traits and mental health assessed at W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, data on life satisfaction collected at W3 to W9, and data on life events collected at W1 to W9.
ALLS included participants (a) living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, (b) aged between 18 and 21 years at W1, and (c) speaking at least basic English.
Overall, 3,048 individuals took part in W1, of which 700 could not be reached again at W2.
A booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3.

In addition to basic data quality checks by the ALLS investigators (see https://osf.io/7pmh4/files/gjnqh for details), we excluded participants if they failed all attention-check items at W1 (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items; "for this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate").
text.formatted: In addition to basic data quality checks by the ALLS investigators (see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/7pmh4/files/gjnqh">https://osf.io/7pmh4/files/gjnqh</ref> for details), we excluded participants if they failed all attention-check items at W1 (as some participants did not seem to understand this type of attention check items; "for this item, please tick the box for slightly inaccurate").

text.text: At later waves, where improved quality check items were used (W3, W5, W7, W9), we excluded participants who failed at least one attention check item (e.g., "Hello, are you still paying attention?
Which of the following is an animal? -House, tree, plane, cat, book").
Applying these exclusion criteria led to the following sample sizes across waves: NW1 = 2,721, NW2 = 2,281, NW3 = 2,046, NW4 = 2,858, NW5 = 2,382, NW6 = 2,624, NW7 = 2,057, NW8 = 2,818, NW9 = 2,101.
At W1, participants were on average 18.30 years old (SD = 0.72).
Participants were approximately equally distributed across the three countries (Kenya: 34%, Namibia: 33%, South Africa: 33%), 56% of the sample were female, and 67% had high school level education.
At W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, agency and communion were assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: At W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, agency and communion were assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Thalmayer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The 45 items (e.g., "I tend to be calm") were assessed on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate).
We reverse-scored nine inverted agency items and seven inverted communion items and calculated mean scores (agency: α = .78, communion: α = .86).
From W3 to W9, life satisfaction was assessed with the three-item version of the Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; Kjell & Diener, 2021).
text.formatted: From W3 to W9, life satisfaction was assessed with the three-item version of the Satisfaction With Life Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Diener et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kjell & Diener, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Items (e.g., "I am satisfied with my life") were assessed on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) and we calculated mean scores for the analyses (α = .71).
At W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, mental health problems were assessed with the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: At W1, W3, W5, W7, and W9, mental health problems were assessed with the International Mental Health Assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Thalmayer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Items (e.g., "I felt scared") were assessed on a 7-point scale ranging from 0 (not in the last month/never) to 6 (daily).
To ease comparability with the other constructs, we reverse scored this scale so that higher values indicated better mental health (α = .95).

We used all items of this questionnaire to create an overall score for mental health except for one substance use item ("I had 3 or more alcoholic beverages in a day") and one relationship conflict item ("I argued with friends or family") that had been shown to generalize poorly across the three countries included in the ALLS (Hofmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We used all items of this questionnaire to create an overall score for mental health except for one substance use item ("I had 3 or more alcoholic beverages in a day") and one relationship conflict item ("I argued with friends or family") that had been shown to generalize poorly across the three countries included in the ALLS <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hofmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We used two strategies to identify the occurrence of life events.

Six events, drawn from the Markers of Adulthood (Arnett, 2003), were directly assessed at each wave in a yes/no format: moved away from caregivers, obtained a driver's license, finishing education, start full-time employed, first sexual intercourse, bought a house.
text.formatted: Six events, drawn from the Markers of Adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arnett, 2003)</ref>, were directly assessed at each wave in a yes/no format: moved away from caregivers, obtained a driver's license, finishing education, start full-time employed, first sexual intercourse, bought a house.

text.text: Five other events were identified by examining changes in demographic variables also assessed at each wave.

Specifically, we inferred the occurrences of a new romantic relationship, marriage, and relationship breakup based on changes in participants' relationship status, the occurrence of job loss based on changes in employment status, and childbirth based on an increase in the reported number of own children.
We used R (Version 4.5.3) and R packages plm (Croissant & Millo, 2008), multicomp (Hothorn et al., 2002), tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We used R (Version 4.5.3) and R packages plm <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Croissant & Millo, 2008)</ref>, multicomp <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hothorn et al., 2002)</ref>, tidyverse <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Wickham et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our analyses comprised three steps.
In a first step, we identified the occurrence of the eleven life events of interest as described above.

We only considered event occurrences after W1 in order to have pre-event data and timing information for all event occurrences (e.g., if participants indicated at W1 that they already had their first sexual intercourse, this event was not considered for this person).
Furthermore, we only considered the first occurrence of each event.
For example, if a participant reported multiple marriages, we focused on only the first in our analyses.

Finally, in a deviation from the preregistration, we only considered "robust event occurrences", meaning that we only examined life events where participants indicated in two consecutive assessment waves that they had experienced a certain event.

For example, we did not consider life events where participants reported that they had experienced an event at W3 but did not report the occurrence at W4 (e.g., reporting that they already had intercourse at W3 but not at W4).
We deviated from the preregistration in this way to address inconsistent reporting.
We additionally created control groups for each life event comprising individuals who did not experience the event across the study period but could in principle have experienced it.
Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see Krämer et al., 2025, for a similar approach).
text.formatted: Due to the causal interdependence of some life events, individuals in the control group had to fulfill specific conditions for some life events (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krämer et al., 2025</ref>, for a similar approach).

text.text: Specifically, for the control group of relationship breakup, we only included individuals who reported being in a relationship or married at some point during the study.
Similarly, for the control group of job loss, we only considered individuals who were employed at some point during the study.

Finally, for the events moved away from caregiver, finished education, start full-time employment, first sexual intercourse, and bought a house, we only considered individuals who had not yet experienced these events at W1.
As a second step, we used fixed-effect regressions to examine event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health.
Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences (Allison, 2009).
text.formatted: Fixed-effect regressions include a dummy variable for each individual that captures between-person differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allison, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: These person-specific dummies thus control for the effects of all time-invariant confounders (e.g., country, gender, childhood characteristics).
Fixed-effect regressions are a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026; Krämer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Fixed-effect regressions are a suitable method to investigate within-person changes in response to life events <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krämer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We estimated one model for each event-outcome combination.
Personality trait scores, life satisfaction, and mental health for person i at time point t served as dependent variable (Traitit).
We standardized these outcomes within the overall sample (i.e., across events) to facilitate the comparison of event-related changes across events.
Time from and to event occurrence served as predictors.

Specifically, we included five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables that captured within-person changes 2 years before the event (D-2Y), 1 year before the event (D-1Y), up to 1 year after the event (D+1Y), 2 years after the event (D+2Y), and more than 2 years after the event (D>+2Y).
text.formatted: Specifically, we included five discrete and mutually exclusive dummy variables that captured within-person changes 2 years before the event (D-2Y), 1 year before the event (D-1Y), up to 1 year after the event (D+1Y), 2 years after the event (D+2Y), and more than 2 years after the event (D>+2Y).

text.text: Using these dummies allowed us to estimate withinperson changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health, without assuming a specific functional form.
Furthermore, it allowed us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, it allowed us to compare findings to recent results from Western countries that used the same statistical approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To control for normative changes in the outcomes, we included 𝐴𝑔𝑒 𝑖𝑡 and 𝐴𝑔𝑒 𝑖𝑡 our models.

Finally, in a deviation from the preregistration, we included a testing variable (0 = first assessment of a person,1 = second assessment,2 = third assessment, and so on) to deal with testing-related differences between assessment waves (e.g., see Asselmann & Specht, 2020; Denissen et al., 2019 for similar approaches).
text.formatted: Finally, in a deviation from the preregistration, we included a testing variable (0 = first assessment of a person,1 = second assessment,2 = third assessment, and so on) to deal with testing-related differences between assessment waves (e.g., see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Asselmann & Specht, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Denissen et al., 2019</ref> for similar approaches).

text.text: An example model equation reads as follows: 𝛼 𝑖 represents the person-specific fixed effects that account for stable between-person differences. 𝛽 1 to 𝛽 5 capture event-related changes before and after the event occurrence, whereas 𝛽 6 to 𝛽 8 capture age-or testing-related changes.
We estimated the significance of these effects using cluster-robust standard errors (Arellano method with small sample correction).
To evaluate our hypotheses, we examined the direction and statistical significance of 𝛽 1 to 𝛽 5 .
An effect was interpreted as being in line with our hypotheses, if we observed significant changes in the expected direction for any event-related dummy.
As we thus had five statistical tests to evaluate each hypothesis, we used an adjusted level of significance of α = .05/5 = .01 for our analyses.

Furthermore, we put emphasis on effect sizes in the interpretation of our findings by comparing the size of these effects to event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, we put emphasis on effect sizes in the interpretation of our findings by comparing the size of these effects to event-related changes across outcomes and to results from Western countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Participants belonging to the control group received a zero on all event-related dummies.
These participants thus only contributed to the estimation of the intercept, age-related changes, and the testing variable (Krämer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These participants thus only contributed to the estimation of the intercept, age-related changes, and the testing variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Krämer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As a supplementary analysis, we examined linear contrasts across event-related dummies to examine changes from specific pre-event to specific post-event assessments.
These linear contrasts, for example, informed us whether there are significant changes from assessments 1 year before the event occurrence to 1 year after the event occurrence.
We repeated the analyses from Step 2 using only two instead of five event-related dummies to provide results that are more comparable to simple pre-post analyses (e.g., Bühler et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We repeated the analyses from Step 2 using only two instead of five event-related dummies to provide results that are more comparable to simple pre-post analyses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bühler et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we ran a simplified model with a pre-event dummy (DPre) capturing within-person changes up to 2 years prior to the event occurrence, and a post-event dummy (DPost) capturing changes in assessments after the event occurrence.
The linear contrast of the two dummies (DPre -DPost) allowed us to examine whether there are event-related changes from pre-to post-event assessments.

Although recent research suggests that variation in the scales of the measure we used can be accounted for by a single higher-order factor (Hofmann et al., 2025), lower-order constructs may allow for more nuanced insights into their links with life events.
text.formatted: Although recent research suggests that variation in the scales of the measure we used can be accounted for by a single higher-order factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hofmann et al., 2025)</ref>, lower-order constructs may allow for more nuanced insights into their links with life events.

text.text: Therefore, we repeated the above-described analyses using depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep difficulties, life stress, anger, harmful substance use, interpersonal conflict, and psychosis as lower-level aspects of mental health.

Finally, we also explored whether event-related changes in agency, communion, life satisfaction, and mental health differed between male and female participants and among the three countries included in the ALLS.
To do so, we included interactions between the eventrelated dummies and gender or country into our models.

For these analyses, we drew on the simplified model described in Step 3 because this model had larger sample sizes for each eventrelated dummy and thus resulted in more stable estimates to test these interaction effects.
When preregistering the study (i.e., before determining our final sample size), we conducted approximative power analyses based on paired t-tests using the R package pwr (Champely, 2006).
text.formatted: When preregistering the study (i.e., before determining our final sample size), we conducted approximative power analyses based on paired t-tests using the R package pwr <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Champely, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These power analyses indicated sufficient power (1 -β = 0.80, α = .01) to identify very small event-related changes (d = 0.10) for events with a sample size of n = 1,172, small event-related changes (d = 0.20) for events with a sample size of n = 296, medium eventrelated changes (d = 0.41) for events with n = 73, and strong event-related changes (d = 0.63) for events with n = 33.
We, thus, preregistered to only discuss events for which we could detect at least medium-sized effects (n ≥ 73) in the main manuscript.
Other events were still analyzed but are only reported in the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915).

These samples sizes of the event groups refer to "robust event occurrences", meaning that participants had to report a respective life change at two consecutive assessments.
This way of capturing life events was a deviation from the preregistration to deal with inconsistencies in participants' reporting.
Event-related changes in agency are illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Event-related changes in agency are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: As can be seen in this figure, several life events were associated with significant within-person decreases in agency.

First sexual intercourse predicted decreases in agency in the year before (d = -0.24, p = .003), the year after (d = -0.32, p < .001), and 2 years after the event (d = -0.30, p = .003), with linear contrasts among event-related dummies indicating that agency significantly decreased from assessments 2 years prior the first sexual intercourse to assessments up to 2 years thereafter.
text.formatted: First sexual intercourse predicted decreases in agency in the year before (d = -0.24, p = .003), the year after (d = -0.32, p < .001), and 2 years after the event (d = -0.30, p = .003), with linear contrasts among event-related dummies indicating that agency significantly decreased from assessments 2 years prior the first sexual intercourse to assessments up to 2 years thereafter.

text.text: Furthermore, we found significant within-person decreases in agency in the year before childbirth (d = -0.32, p = .005), 2 years before a relationship breakup (d = -0.22, p = .002), 1 year before getting a driver's license (d = -0.48, p = .003), and 1 year after graduation (d = -0.20, p = .008).

Finally, moving away from the caregiver was associated with event-related changes in agency in the year before (d = -0.27, p = .002) and the year after (d = -0.27, p = .001) the event occurrence, with linear contrasts pointing to a significant decrease in agency from 2 years before moving away from caregiver to assessments 1 year thereafter.
Most of these effects were replicated in the simplified model that only considered prevs. post-event changes.

Specifically, we found significant decreases in agency after the first sexual intercourse (d = -0.32, p < .001) and after moving away from the caregiver (d = -0.24, p = .003), as well as decreases before childbirth (d = -0.29, p = .005) and a relationship breakup (d = -0.21, p = .001).
text.formatted: Specifically, we found significant decreases in agency after the first sexual intercourse (d = -0.32, p < .001) and after moving away from the caregiver (d = -0.24, p = .003), as well as decreases before childbirth (d = -0.29, p = .005) and a relationship breakup (d = -0.21, p = .001).

text.text: Overall, our findings were in line with Hypothesis 2 that childbirth predicts decreases in agency, while Hypothesis 1 (marriage predicts decreases in agency) could not be formally tested due to the low sample size for this event.

Event-related changes in communion are illustrated in Figure 2.
text.formatted: Event-related changes in communion are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Similar to the effects for agency, several life events predicted within-person decreases in communion.
First, communion decreased in the year before a relationship breakup (d = -0.22, p = .004).
Second, finishing education predicted decreases in communion in the year before (d = -0.28, p < .001) and the year after (d = -0.23, p = .003) the event occurrence.
text.formatted: Second, finishing education predicted decreases in communion in the year before (d = -0.28, p < .001) and the year after (d = -0.23, p = .003) the event occurrence.

text.text: Finally, there were significant within-person decreases in communion 1 year before (d = -0.51, p < .001), 1 year after (d = -0.48, p = .001), 2 years after (d = -0.42, p = .004), and more than 2 years (d = -0.56, p = .001) after obtaining a driver's license.
text.formatted: Finally, there were significant within-person decreases in communion 1 year before (d = -0.51, p < .001), 1 year after (d = -0.48, p = .001), 2 years after (d = -0.42, p = .004), and more than 2 years (d = -0.56, p = .001) after obtaining a driver's license.

text.text: All of these effects were replicated in the simplified model (-0.44 ≤ d ≤ -0.20).
In addition, we found significant decreases in communion after the first sexual intercourse in that model (d = -0.24, p = .007).
In sum, findings were not in line with Hypothesis 4 (start full-time employed predicts increases in communion) and contrary to Hypothesis 3 (finishing education predicts increases in communion).

Event-related changes in life satisfaction are illustrated in Figure 3.
text.formatted: Event-related changes in life satisfaction are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Life satisfaction significantly increased 2 years before (d = 0.25, p < .001), 1 year before (d = 0.34, p < .001), 1 year after (d = 0.39, p < .001), 2 years after (d = 0.49, p < .001), and more than 2 years after (d = 0.50, p < .001) obtaining a driver's license.
text.formatted: Life satisfaction significantly increased 2 years before (d = 0.25, p < .001), 1 year before (d = 0.34, p < .001), 1 year after (d = 0.39, p < .001), 2 years after (d = 0.49, p < .001), and more than 2 years after (d = 0.50, p < .001) obtaining a driver's license.

text.text: In addition, linear contrasts among eventrelated dummies indicated changes in life satisfaction from specific pre-event to specific postevent assessments.

For example, life satisfaction significantly increased from assessments 1 to 2 years prior to a new romantic relationship to assessments more than 2 years thereafter, whereas life satisfaction significantly decreased from assessments 1 to 2 years prior to job loss to assessments 1 year thereafter.
Similarly, life satisfaction significantly increased from the year before starting full-time employment to assessments 1 to 2 years thereafter.

While similar effects emerged for linear contrasts between pre-and post-event dummies in the simplified model, the within-person increases in life satisfaction surrounding obtaining a driver's license were not replicated.

Overall, findings were partially in line with Hypothesis 5 (new romantic relationship predicts increases in life satisfaction), Hypothesis 10 (starting fulltime employed predicts increases in life satisfaction), and Hypothesis 11 (job loss predicts decreases in life satisfaction), whereas we found no supporting evidence for Hypothesis 7 (childbirth predicts increases in life satisfaction), Hypothesis 8 (relationship breakup predicts decreases in life satisfaction), and Hypothesis 9 (finishing education predicts increases in life satisfaction).
Hypothesis 6 (marriage predicts increases in life satisfaction) could not be formally tested due to the low sample size for this event.

text.text: The only event significantly related to within-person changes in mental health was first sexual intercourse.

Specifically, mental health significantly decreased 2 years before (d = -0.23, p = .007), 1 year before (d = -0.31, p = .001), 1 year after (d = -0.42, p < .001), 2 years after (d = -0.38, p < .001), and more than 2 years after (d = -0.37, p = .001) first sexual intercourse.

text.text: This effect was replicated in the simplified model, indicating significant decreases in mental health before (d = -0.28, p < .001) and after (d = -0.41, p < .001) having first sexual intercourse.

text.text: These findings were thus not in line with any of the preregistered hypotheses.
In exploratory analyses, we examined event-related changes in specific mental health problems.

These analyses showed that the decreases in mental health in the years surrounding first sexual intercourse were primarily driven by increases in depression, anxiety, life stress, and interpersonal conflicts but not-for example-sleep issues and anger issues.

In addition, we found increases in substance abuse in the years surrounding graduation and increases in anxiety in the years surrounding obtaining a driver's license (see Section 4 of the https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915 for details).
text.formatted: In addition, we found increases in substance abuse in the years surrounding graduation and increases in anxiety in the years surrounding obtaining a driver's license (see Section 4 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915">Supplementary Materials</ref> for details).

text.text: In an additional exploratory analysis step, we examined whether event-related changes differed between men and women and among the three countries included in ALLS.
Results of this analysis can be found in Section 5 of the https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915.
text.formatted: Results of this analysis can be found in Section 5 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915">Supplementary Materials</ref>.

text.text: Overall, we found limited evidence for gender differences in event-related changes.
The only exception was that women decreased more in their communion after their first sexual intercourse than men.
Furthermore, we found several differences in event-related changes across the three countries.
For example, emerging adults living in Kenya showed stronger agency decreases after experiencing a relationship breakup or finishing education than emerging adults in South Africa.
Similarly, emerging adults living in Kenya showed stronger decreases in their communion after a new relationship or childbirth than emerging adults in Namibia.

The present study is one of the first examinations of event-related changes in sub-Saharan Africa.

Using data from young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we found that agency and/or communion decreased among individuals who became a parent, finished education, or obtained a driver's license.
Furthermore, life satisfaction increased for participants getting their driver's license, and mental health decreased in the years surrounding their first sexual intercourse.
In the following, we discuss different possible interpretations of our results and reasons why event-related changes may have diverged from those reported in Western contexts.

The key take-away of this study is that event-related changes in personality traits, mental health, and life satisfaction seem to differ across cultural contexts as only one of our generalizability hypotheses was supported.
The only finding that converged with prior metaanalyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The only finding that converged with prior metaanalyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bühler et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Becoming a parent and caring for an infant is associated with new responsibilities and challenges, which may undermine feelings of competence and confidence, and decrease opportunities to show agentic behaviors such as asserting oneself at work or going out with friends.
Other events substantially diverged in their effects from Western findings.
For example, finishing education predicted decreases rather than increases in agency and communion.
There may be methodological or substantive reasons for these differences.
Methodologically, emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa may be less experienced with filling out questionnaires than over-researched student samples from Western countries.

This could lead to differences in response biases, socially desirable responding, and willingness to disclose personal experiences (e.g., Tellis & Chandrasekaran, 2010), all of which may influence results on event-related changes in personality and well-being.
text.formatted: This could lead to differences in response biases, socially desirable responding, and willingness to disclose personal experiences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Tellis & Chandrasekaran, 2010)</ref>, all of which may influence results on event-related changes in personality and well-being.

text.text: Furthermore, linguistic misunderstandings may have resulted in inconsistent reporting of life events, potentially blurring results on event-related changes, which is why we decided to focus on events that were consistently reported in our main analyses.
Substantively, there may be differences in the meaning of life events across cultural contexts.

For example, while finishing education is often viewed as a positive milestone associated with employment, financial independence, and adult role attainment in Western countries, these outcomes may not always be readily accessible to emerging adults in contexts characterized by high unemployment and economic uncertainty (Levy & Dubinsky, 2024).
text.formatted: For example, while finishing education is often viewed as a positive milestone associated with employment, financial independence, and adult role attainment in Western countries, these outcomes may not always be readily accessible to emerging adults in contexts characterized by high unemployment and economic uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Levy & Dubinsky, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa, finishing education may signal entry into a period of uncertainty during which anticipated opportunities fail to materialize, potentially undermining agency and communion.

Supporting this interpretation, decreases in agency after finishing education were highest for young adults living in Kenya, the ALLS country with the highest youth unemployment rate (Federation of Kenya Employers, 2024).
Similarly, first sexual intercourse seems to differ in its mental health implications across cultural contexts.

In Western countries, first sexual intercourse tends to be either unrelated to well-being or associated with transient increases in life satisfaction and self-esteem-consistent with the fulfillment of a developmental milestone (Andrae et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In Western countries, first sexual intercourse tends to be either unrelated to well-being or associated with transient increases in life satisfaction and self-esteem-consistent with the fulfillment of a developmental milestone <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andrae et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, mental health significantly decreased in the years surrounding first sexual intercourse in young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa.

There is initial evidence from South Africa indicating that the circumstances surrounding the sexual debut which can include coercion, sexual violence, and health risks are important in understanding this association (McClinton Appollis et al., 2022; Seff et al., 2021).
text.formatted: There is initial evidence from South Africa indicating that the circumstances surrounding the sexual debut which can include coercion, sexual violence, and health risks are important in understanding this association <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(McClinton Appollis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Seff et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: First sexual intercourse may be associated with poorer mental health where it occurs within contexts of coercion and adverse health consequences.
Overall, our pattern of results points to broader cross-cultural differences in the developmental significance of emerging adulthood.

While emerging adulthood is typically seen as a phase of exploration and growth in Western countries (Arnett, 2007), structural barriers and constraints may complicate these developmental trajectories in sub-Saharan Africa.
text.formatted: While emerging adulthood is typically seen as a phase of exploration and growth in Western countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arnett, 2007)</ref>, structural barriers and constraints may complicate these developmental trajectories in sub-Saharan Africa.

text.text: This interpretation is also consistent with the concept of Waithood (Honwana, 2019), which describes emerging adulthood in sub-Saharan Africa as a a prolonged and often involuntary period between socially recognized adulthood and dependence due to structural and economic constraints.
text.formatted: This interpretation is also consistent with the concept of Waithood <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Honwana, 2019)</ref>, which describes emerging adulthood in sub-Saharan Africa as a a prolonged and often involuntary period between socially recognized adulthood and dependence due to structural and economic constraints.

text.text: However, it is also noteworthy that some event-related changes-especially those in life satisfaction and mental health-did not follow the typical adaptation pattern, with the most pronounced effects in the first year after the event occurrence, then slowly attenuating (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026; Krämer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, it is also noteworthy that some event-related changes-especially those in life satisfaction and mental health-did not follow the typical adaptation pattern, with the most pronounced effects in the first year after the event occurrence, then slowly attenuating <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Krämer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This raises questions about whether these events were responsible for the observed changes, or whether they are proxies for other changes.

We aimed to come close to the causal relevance of life events by accounting for stable betweenperson differences with fixed-effects regressions and controlling for within-person age and testing effects.
However, other experiences that co-occur with the examined life events could still confound the observed effects.

For example, improvements in the financial situation may predict both getting a driver's license-as driving lessons are relatively costly-and increases in life satisfaction, which could explain why we found increases in life satisfaction when participants obtained their driver's license.
Future research should therefore investigate how emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa experience important life events and how these events are associated with changes in their everyday lives.
The present study has several limitations.
First, although the overall sample size of ALLS is relatively large, the sample size for specific events was sometimes limited.
For example, we could not test our hypotheses for getting married as this event was too rare in the examined age group.
Second, by relying on demographic status changes and a fixed set of directly measured life events, we may have missed other contextually important life changes (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Second, by relying on demographic status changes and a fixed set of directly measured life events, we may have missed other contextually important life changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Third, we exclusively relied on self-reports to examine event-related changes, which are prone to biases such as socially desirable responding or acquiescence.
Life events have been theorized to be important drivers of changes in personality traits and well-being.
However, prior evidence on these effects stemmed almost exclusively from Western countries.

Using a large longitudinal sample of young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we examined the cross-cultural generalizability of event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health.
Although we found several significant event-related changes, findings diverged substantially from Western results.
Future crosscultural research is needed to test the replicability of our findings and to investigate different explanations for why findings may differ across cultural contexts.
